arXiv:2506.13010v1 [math.NT] 16 Jun 2025

On polynomial progressions via transference

Daniel Altman Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 380, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Email address: daniel.h.altman@gmail.com and Mehtaab Sawhney Address: Department of Mathematics, Columbia University, New York, NY 10027 Email address: m.sawhney@columbia.edu
Abstract.

We prove new cases of reasonable bounds for the polynomial Szemerédi theorem both over ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} with NN prime and over the integers. In particular, we prove reasonable bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem in the integers with fixed polynomial common difference. That is, we prove for any polynomial P⁡(y)∈ℤ⁡[y]P(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0, that the largest subset A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N] avoiding the pattern

x,x+P⁡(y),…,x+k​P​(y)x,x+P(y),\ldots,x+kP(y)

has size bounded by ≪P,kN(logloglogN)−ΩP,k​(1).\ll_{P,k}N(\log\log\log N)^{-\Omega_{P,k}(1)}.

1. Introduction

Consider any set of distinct polynomials P1​(y),…,Pt​(y)∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1}(y),\ldots,P_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with Pj​(0)=0P_{j}(0)=0 for each jj. Let rP1,…,Pt​([N])r_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}}([N]) denote the size of largest subset AA of [N]:={1,…,N}[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\} avoiding nontrivial copies of the pattern

x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y).x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y).

By nontrivial pattern here we require that Pi​(y)−Pj​(y)≠0P_{i}(y)-P_{j}(y)\neq 0 for all i≠ji\neq j. The celebrated polynomial Szemerédi theorem of Bergelson and Leibman [2] states that

rP1,…,Pt​([N])=oP1,…,Pt​(N).r_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}}([N])=o_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}}(N).

Due to the use of ergodic techniques the results of Bergelson and Leibman [2] are qualitative and give no effective bounds for the rate of decay of rP1,…,Pt​([N])/Nr_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}}([N])/N. In the case of Szemerédi’s theorem [42, 43], seminal work of Gowers [6, 8] proved that

ry,…,k​y​([N])≪N​(log⁡log⁡N)−Ωk​(1).r_{y,\ldots,ky}([N])\ll N(\log\log N)^{-\Omega_{k}(1)}.

However, progress towards genuinely polynomial cases of the polynomial Szemerédi’s theorem remained more limited and was highlighted by Gowers [7] as a problem of interest. Results of Sarközy [41] gave effective bounds for the pattern x,x+y2x,x+y^{2} via the circle method. The underlying method has been generalized to give effective bounds for the case of x,x+P⁡(y)x,x+P(y) when P⁡(y)∈ℤ⁡[y]P(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0 by Lucier [30].11 1 This result applies more generally to the case where P⁡(y)P(y) is intersective. P⁡(y)P(y) is said to be intersective if for all integers q≥1q\geq 1 there is n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z} such that q|P⁡(n)q|P(n).

The cases where the underlying pattern contains more than two terms proved more difficult. A result of Green handled the case of three–term arithmetic progressions where the underlying difference was a sum of two squares [9]. A result of Prendiville [40] handled the case of kk-term arithmetic progressions where the common difference is a perfect power. These results however both relied on homogeneity to pass to “perfect power” differences in order to run a density increment strategy. Therefore it was a substantial breakthrough when Peluse and Prendiville [38, 37] provided effective bounds for the case of x,x+y,x+y2x,x+y,x+y^{2}. This was extended substantially in work of Peluse [36] to the case of x,x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y)x,x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y) where the Pj​(y)P_{j}(y) are of differing degrees. Finally, work of Peluse, Sah and the second author [39] handled the case of 33-term arithmetic progressions with difference y2−1y^{2}-1, and this was extended to general P⁡(y)P(y) with a simple integer root implicitly in work of Kravitz, Kuca and Leng [17].

The first result of this paper is a version of Szemerédi’s theorem allowing for the difference to be equal to any fixed polynomial difference.

Theorem 1.1.

Fix a polynomial P⁡(y)∈ℤ⁡[y]P(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0. Let a→=(a1,…,at)∈ℤt\vec{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t})\in\mathbb{Z}^{t} with ai≠aja_{i}\neq a_{j} for i≠ji\neq j. Then there exists c=c⁡(deg⁡(P),t)>0c=c(\operatorname{deg}(P),t)>0 such that the following hold.

  • •

    If t=3t=3 and P′​(0)≠0P^{\prime}(0)\neq 0 then

    ra1​P,…,at​P([N])≪P,a→Nexp(−c(loglogN)c).r_{a_{1}P,\ldots,a_{t}P}([N])\ll_{P,\vec{a}}N\exp(-c(\log\log N)^{c}).
  • •

    If P′​(0)≠0P^{\prime}(0)\neq 0 then

    ra1​P,…,at​P([N])≪P,a→Nexp(−c(logloglogN)c).r_{a_{1}P,\ldots,a_{t}P}([N])\ll_{P,\vec{a}}N\exp(-c(\log\log\log N)^{c}).
  • •

    If P′​(0)=0P^{\prime}(0)=0 then

    ra1​P,…,at​P([N])≪P,a→N(logloglogN)−c.r_{a_{1}P,\ldots,a_{t}P}([N])\ll_{P,\vec{a}}N(\log\log\log N)^{-c}.
Remark 1.2.

The final item in this theorem can likely be improved via improving a result of Prendiville [40] which handles the case P⁡(y)=ykP(y)=y^{k} and invoking recent results regarding the inverse theorem for the Gowers norm [28]. We refer the reader to Remark 2.12.

We also consider the polynomial Szemerédi theorem over ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} where NN is prime. This model setting is often simpler than the corresponding setting over the integers as the image of a polynomial Q⁡(y)Q(y) over ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} is dense. Given a sequence of polynomials Q1​(y),…,Qt​(y)Q_{1}(y),\ldots,Q_{t}(y), we define rQ1,…,Qt​(ℤ/N​ℤ)r_{Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{t}}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}) to be the size of the largest subset of ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} avoiding copies of

x+Q1​(y),…,x+Qt​(y)x+Q_{1}(y),\ldots,x+Q_{t}(y)

with x∈ℤ/N​ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} and y∈ℤ/N​ℤy\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} such that Qi​(y)−Qj​(y)≠0Q_{i}(y)-Q_{j}(y)\neq 0 for all i≠ji\neq j.

In ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}, the first progress was due to work of Bourgain and Chang [3], giving quantitative bounds for r0,y,y2​(ℤ/N​ℤ)r_{0,y,y^{2}}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}). This was generalized in work of Peluse [34] and independently Dong, Li and Sawin [5] to r0,Q1​(y),Q2​(y)​(ℤ/N​ℤ)r_{0,Q_{1}(y),Q_{2}(y)}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}) if Q1Q_{1} and Q2Q_{2} are linearly independent. These results were greatly extended in work of Peluse [35] to x,x+Q1​(y),…,x+Qt​(y)x,x+Q_{1}(y),\ldots,x+Q_{t}(y) where QiQ_{i} are linearly independent. Notably, this work introduced the degree lowering method which was subsequently used over the integers. There are also additional results of Kuca [19] which, for example, covers the case of x,x+y,…,x+(m−1)​y,x+ym,…,x+ym+k−1x,x+y,\ldots,x+(m-1)y,x+y^{m},\ldots,x+y^{m+k-1} and work of Leng [26] which handles the case of x,x+P⁡(y),x+Q⁡(y),x+P⁡(y)+Q⁡(y)x,x+P(y),x+Q(y),x+P(y)+Q(y).

Our second result provides a unified framework which proves all known cases of effective bounds in the polynomial Szemerédi theorem, as well as proving several new cases. Furthermore these results essentially resolve several conjectures of Leng [26, Conjecture 1–3] (although as stated there are counterexamples to [26, Conjecture 1]).

To state our results, we will require the notions of a kernel system and homogeneous polynomial patterns, and will introduce the notion of a transferable polynomial pattern. The first two were considered in work of Kuca [20] while the third arises when we apply transference.

We first define the kernel system of a set of polynomials.

Definition 1.3.

Given polynomials P1,…,Pt∈ℤ⁡[x1,…,xk]P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}\in\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}], the kernel system κ⁡(𝒫)\kappa(\mathcal{P}) of pattern 𝒫=(P1,…,Pt)\mathcal{P}=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}) is the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space of tuples of polynomials Q→=(Q1,…,Qt)∈ℚ⁡[z]\vec{Q}=(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{t})\in\mathbb{Q}[z] such that

∑i=1tQi​(Pi​(x1,…,xk))=0.\sum_{i=1}^{t}Q_{i}(P_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}))=0.

We now define the notions of homogeneous and transferable polynomial patterns.

Definition 1.4.

Consider 𝒫=(x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y))∈ℤ⁡[x,y]\mathcal{P}=(x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y))\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] with Pi​(0)=0P_{i}(0)=0 and PiP_{i} distinct. Let d=maxi∈[t]⁡deg⁡Pid=\max_{i\in[t]}\deg P_{i} and define the (unique) homogeneous linear polynomials Pi∗∈ℤ⁡[y1,…,yd]P_{i}^{\ast}\in\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},\ldots,y_{d}] such that

Pi∗​(y,y2,…,yd)=Pi​(y).P_{i}^{\ast}(y,y^{2},\ldots,y^{d})=P_{i}(y).

We say that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is transferable if whenever Q→=(Q1,…,Qt)∈κ⁡(𝒫)\vec{Q}=(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{t})\in\kappa(\mathcal{P}) holds we must in fact have

∑i=1tQi​(x+Pi∗​(y1,…,yd))=0.\sum_{i=1}^{t}Q_{i}(x+P_{i}^{\ast}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{d}))=0.

We say that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is homogeneous if κ⁡(𝒫)\kappa(\mathcal{P}) is spanned by tuples of the form (c1​zi,…,ct​zi)(c_{1}z^{i},\ldots,c_{t}z^{i}).

Remark 1.5.

By way of example, observe that the polynomial pattern 𝒫1=(x,x+y,x+2​y,x+y2)\mathcal{P}_{1}=(x,x+y,x+2y,x+y^{2}) is not homogeneous due to the following identity:

2​(x+y2)=2​x+x2−2​(x+y)2+(x+2​y)2.2(x+y^{2})=2x+x^{2}-2(x+y)^{2}+(x+2y)^{2}.

We next have the existence of polynomial patterns which are not transferable, but which are homogeneous. In particular, consider 𝒫2=(x,x−y2,x+y2,x+y,x+y3,x+y+y3)\mathcal{P}_{2}=(x,x-y^{2},x+y^{2},x+y,x+y^{3},x+y+y^{3}) and observe that

(x+y2)2−2​x2+(x−y2)2=(x+y+y3)2−(x+y3)2−(x+y)2+x2=2​y4.(x+y^{2})^{2}-2x^{2}+(x-y^{2})^{2}=(x+y+y^{3})^{2}-(x+y^{3})^{2}-(x+y)^{2}+x^{2}=2y^{4}.

Finally we have that all transferable patterns are homogeneous: the kernel system of a set of linear patterns is easily seen to be spanned by tuples of the form (c1​zi,…,ct​zi)(c_{1}z^{i},\ldots,c_{t}z^{i}) by considering the degree of terms arising in a relation determined by Q→∈κ⁡(𝒫)\vec{Q}\in\kappa(\mathcal{P}).

The main result of this work over finite fields is the following transference result.

Theorem 1.6.

Let Pi​(y)∈ℤ​[y]P_{i}(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with Pi​(0)=0P_{i}(0)=0 and suppose that 𝒫=(x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y))\mathcal{P}=(x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y)) is transferable. Let d=max1≤i≤t⁡deg⁡(Pi)d=\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\operatorname{deg}(P_{i}) and define Pi∗​(y1,…,yd)P_{i}^{\ast}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{d}) as in Definition 1.4. Let NN be prime and consider fi:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf_{i}:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} with ∥fi∥∞≤1\lVert f_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1.

There exists c=c1.6​(P1,…,Pt)>0c=c_{\ref{thm:main-poly}}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{t})>0 such that

|𝔼x,y∈ℤ/N​ℤ∏i=1tfi(x+Pi(y))−𝔼x,y1,…,yd∈ℤ/N​ℤ∏i=1tfi(x+Pi∗(y1,…,yd))|≪𝒫exp(−c(loglogN)c).\Big|\mathbb{E}_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+P_{i}(y))-\mathbb{E}_{x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{d}\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+P_{i}^{\ast}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{d}))\Big|\ll_{\mathcal{P}}\exp(-c(\log\log N)^{c}).

Therefore there exists c′=c1.6′​(P1,…,Pt)>0c^{\prime}=c_{\ref{thm:main-poly}}^{\prime}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{t})>0 such that if 𝒫\mathcal{P} is transferable then

r𝒫(ℤ/Nℤ)≪𝒫Nexp(−c′(logloglogN)c′).r_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})\ll_{\mathcal{P}}N\exp(-c^{\prime}(\log\log\log N)^{c^{\prime}}).

1.1. Proof outline

The proof of both Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.6 rely on the use of transference to deduce our results regarding polynomial patterns from supersaturation results on other patterns. This general scheme of comparing counts and then applying supersaturation results stems from work of Wooley and Ziegler [46] regarding finding patterns x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y)x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y) where yy is additionally one less than a prime. This idea of transference has now been applied in the context of the polynomial Szemerédi theorem in several instances including work of Kuca [19], Leng [26] and Peluse, Sah and the second author [39]. The main technical improvement in our work is avoiding the use of degree–lowering and instead noting that the required transference claim follows if it holds for nilsequences. We reduce to the more algebraic problem of nilsequence analysis via an iterative application of stashing and applications of the inverse theorem. The algebraic problem is then solved via adapting the arguments of the first author [1] to transferable polynomial patterns.

We first outline the proof of Theorem 1.6 and then briefly discuss the technical differences which arise when handling Theorem 1.1. For the sake of concreteness consider the case of x,x+y,x+2​y,x+y3,x+2​y3x,x+y,x+2y,x+y^{3},x+2y^{3}. Let fi:ℤ/Nℤ→ℂ,i=1,…5f_{i}:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C},\ i=1,\ldots 5 be one-bounded, that is, ∥fi∥∞≤1\lVert f_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1. We wish to upper bound the difference

|𝔼[f1(x)f2(x+y)\displaystyle\Big|\mathbb{E}[f_{1}(x)f_{2}(x+y) f3(x+2y)f4(x+y3)f5(x+2y3)]\displaystyle f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+y^{3})f_{5}(x+2y^{3})]
(1.1) −𝔼[f1(x)f2(x+y)f3(x+2y)f4(x+z)f5(x+2z)]|.\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}[f_{1}(x)f_{2}(x+y)f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+z)f_{5}(x+2z)]\Big|.

Given an appropriate upper bound, the claim about the polynomial Szemerédi theorem then follows from supersaturation results for variants of Szemerédi’s theorem for linear patterns.

Suppose that

δ\displaystyle\delta ≤|𝔼⁡[f1​(x)​f2​(x+y)​f3​(x+2​y)​f4​(x+y3)​f5​(x+2​y3)]\displaystyle\leq\Big|\mathbb{E}[f_{1}(x)f_{2}(x+y)f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+y^{3})f_{5}(x+2y^{3})]
−𝔼[f1(x)f2(x+y)f3(x+2y)f4(x+z)f5(x+2z)]|.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\mathbb{E}[f_{1}(x)f_{2}(x+y)f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+z)f_{5}(x+2z)]\Big|.

𝒟1​(x)=𝔼y,z​(f2​(x+y)​f3​(x+2​y)​f4​(x+y3)​f5​(x+2​y3)−f2​(x+y)​f3​(x+2​y)​f4​(x+z)​f5​(x+2​z)).\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y,z}(f_{2}(x+y)f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+y^{3})f_{5}(x+2y^{3})-f_{2}(x+y)f_{3}(x+2y)f_{4}(x+z)f_{5}(x+2z)).

This is now a largely algebraic problem of comparing the orbits of the polynomial sequences g1​(x,y)=(g⁡(x),g⁡(x+y),g⁡(x+2​y),g⁡(x+y3),g⁡(x+2​y3))g_{1}(x,y)=(g(x),g(x+y),g(x+2y),g(x+y^{3}),g(x+2y^{3})) and g2​(x,y)=(g⁡(x),g⁡(x+y),g⁡(x+2​y),g⁡(x+z),g⁡(x+2​z))g_{2}(x,y)=(g(x),g(x+y),g(x+2y),g(x+z),g(x+2z)) on a nilmanifold of the form G5/Γ5G^{5}/\Gamma^{5}. Crucially, if g:ℤ→Gg:\mathbb{Z}\to G is suitably irrational, it transpires that g1​(x,y)g_{1}(x,y) and g2​(x,y)g_{2}(x,y) equidistribute on the same Leibman nilmanifold GΨ/ΓΨ≤G5/Γ5G^{\Psi}/\Gamma^{\Psi}\leq G^{5}/\Gamma^{5}. Such a result is proven without a quantitative treatment by Kuca [20, Theorem 5.3]. We provide a differing treatment of this result, utilizing the perspective in work of the first author [1] in order to give quantitative bounds. We remark here that our analysis proceeds via a reduction to “totally equidistributed” nilsequences; for further improvements to quantitative aspects it may be interesting to prove such a comparison via a “step reduction” procedure.

The proof of Theorem 1.1 proceeds in a broadly similar manner; however certain technical differences arise in the course of the proof. First various algebraic considerations are simpler in this setting as we wish to compare the orbit (g⁡(x+a1​P​(y)),…,g⁡(x+at​P​(y)))(g(x+a_{1}P(y)),\ldots,g(x+a_{t}P(y))) to that of OPEN(g⁡(x+a1​y)),…,g⁡(x+at​y))(g(x+a_{1}y)),\ldots,g(x+a_{t}y)). For our purposes, we may in fact fix xx and then compare orbits of the form g∗​(y)g^{\ast}(y) and g∗​(P​(y))g^{\ast}(P(y)), which substantially simplifies matters.

This brief summary omits a number of technical details present over the integers which do not arise in the model setting of ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}. We first introduce an archimedean weight on the associated measure for yy (as in [39]); this accounts for the fact that as yy grows the spacing of the polynomial P⁡(y)P(y) grows. Next when operating over the integers, pp-adic biases of P⁡(y)P(y) arise, which we handle via the WW-trick of Green [10]. This however is an oversimplification: observe that if P′​(0)=0P^{\prime}(0)=0 but P′′​(0)≠0P^{\prime\prime}(0)\neq 0 then comparing a WW-trick version of P⁡(y)P(y) with yy is not prudent as they do not agree pp-adically. In this case, one may hope to first apply the WW-trick to P⁡(y)P(y) and then compare the underlying progression to arithmetic progressions with square common difference. This nearly works; however, if P⁡(y)=y2−y4P(y)=y^{2}-y^{4} (say), observe that the common difference under consideration is almost always negative, and yet the transferred progression has positive common difference. This tension at “infinity” and pp-adically requires us to find positivity from an additional pattern before comparing. In particular, instead of comparing differences coming from the WW-tricked version of P⁡(y)=y2−y4P(y)=y^{2}-y^{4} (which is y2−W2​y4y^{2}-W^{2}y^{4}) with y2y^{2}, we compare it with y2​(−W​z+1)y^{2}(-Wz+1). This requires bootstrapping Prendiville’s result [40] to obtain positivity for arithmetic progressions with common difference (−W​z+1)​y2(-Wz+1)y^{2} and then comparing to this modified pattern.

1.2. Organization of the paper and notation

We prove Theorem 1.1 in Section 2 and prove Theorem 1.6 in Section 3. Various tools are developed within subsections; we refer to the beginning of each section for more refined outlines thereof. Throughout the paper we assume familiarity with various concepts associated with nilsequences. These conventions are developed in Appendix A.

We use standard asymptotic notation for functions on ℕ\mathbb{N} throughout. Given functions f=f⁡(x)f=f(x) and g=g⁡(x)g=g(x), we write f=O⁡(g)f=O(g), f≪gf\ll g, or g≫fg\gg f to mean that there is a constant CC such that |f⁡(x)|≤C​g​(x)|f(x)|\leq Cg(x) for sufficiently large xx. Subscripts indicate dependence on parameters. Additionally we let [X]={1,…,⌊X⌋}[X]=\{1,\ldots,\lfloor X\rfloor\} and [±X]={−⌊X⌋,…,⌊X⌋}[\pm X]=\{-\lfloor X\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor X\rfloor\}.

2. Transference in the integers

In this section we prove Theorem 1.1. In the first subsection Section 2.1, we prove various pp-adic comparison results between polynomials. These results are essentially extensions of classical Hensel lifting arguments. The second subsection Section 2.2 introduces Gowers and Gowers–Peluse norms formally and deduces Gowers norm control for the relevant operators. While Gowers norm control follows immediately for the operator with differences P⁡(y)P(y) via the work of Peluse [36], deducing the appropriate Gowers norm control for the operator with differences of the form (±z​W+1)​y2(\pm zW+1)y^{2} requires an additional argument. In Section 2.3, we establish the crucial nilseqeunce comparison result Lemma 2.9. Finally in Section 2.4 we carry out the stashing procedure and deduce Theorem 1.1.

Before proceeding, we reduce to the case where the bottom coefficient of P⁡(y)P(y) is 11. Suppose that P⁡(y)=∑j=d′dbj​yjP(y)=\sum_{j=d^{\prime}}^{d}b_{j}y^{j} with bj∈ℤb_{j}\in\mathbb{Z} where d≥d′≥1d\geq d^{\prime}\geq 1. Firstly note that we may assume that bd′≥1b_{d^{\prime}}\geq 1 by potentially replacing (a1,…,at)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}) with −(a1,…,at)-(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}). We claim that we may in fact assume that bd′=1b_{d^{\prime}}=1 without loss of generality (up to losing a constant factor implicit in Theorem 1.1). To this end observe that

bd′−d′−1​P​(bd′​y)=∑j=d′dbj​yj⋅bd′j−d′−1∈ℤ⁡[y].b_{d^{\prime}}^{-d^{\prime}-1}P(b_{d^{\prime}}y)=\sum_{j=d^{\prime}}^{d}b_{j}y^{j}\cdot b_{d^{\prime}}^{j-d^{\prime}-1}\in\mathbb{Z}[y].

Our claim then follows by subdividing [N][N] into subprogressions with common difference bd′d′+1b_{d^{\prime}}^{d^{\prime}+1}, rescaling, and replacing P⁡(y)P(y) by bd′−d′−1​P​(bd′​y)b_{d^{\prime}}^{-d^{\prime}-1}P(b_{d^{\prime}}y) and NN by ⌊bd′−(d′+1)​N⌋\lfloor b_{d^{\prime}}^{-(d^{\prime}+1)}N\rfloor. Henceforth we assume that bd′=1b_{d^{\prime}}=1.

Lemma 2.1.

Fix a prime pp and let Q⁡(y)=∑j=1dcj​yj∈ℤ⁡[y]Q(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}c_{j}y^{j}\in\mathbb{Z}[y]. Suppose that p|cjp|c_{j} for j≥2j\geq 2 and (c1,p)=1(c_{1},p)=1. Then for all k≥1k\geq 1, we have for all ℓ∈[pk]\ell\in[p^{k}] that

ℙy∈[pk][Q(y)≡ℓmodpk]=p−k.\mathbb{P}_{y\in[p^{k}]}[Q(y)\equiv\ell~\mathrm{mod}~p^{k}]=p^{-k}.

We proceed by induction on kk and note that the base case of k=1k=1 is immediate.

2.2. Gowers norms and transferred operators

We first recall the standard Gowers norm.

Definition 2.3.

Given f:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} and s≥1s\geq 1, we define

∥f∥Us​(ℤ/N​ℤ)2s=𝔼x,h1,…,hs∈ℤ/N​ℤ​Δh1,…,hs​f​(x)\lVert f\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}=\mathbb{E}_{x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}\Delta_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}}f(x)

where Δh​f​(x)=f⁡(x)​f⁡(x+h)¯\Delta_{h}f(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x+h)} is the multiplicative discrete derivative (extended to lists by composition). Given a natural number NN and a function f:[N]→ℂf\colon[N]\to\mathbb{C}, we choose a number N~≥2s​N\widetilde{N}\geq 2^{s}N and define f~:ℤ/N~​ℤ→ℂ\widetilde{f}\colon\mathbb{Z}/\widetilde{N}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} via f~​(x)=f​(x)\widetilde{f}(x)=f(x) for x∈[N]x\in[N] and 00 otherwise. Then

∥f∥Us​[N]:=∥f~∥Us​(ℤ/N~​ℤ)/∥𝟙[N]∥Us​(ℤ/N~​ℤ).\lVert f\rVert_{U^{s}[N]}:=\lVert\widetilde{f}\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z}/\widetilde{N}\mathbb{Z})}/\lVert\mathbbm{1}_{[N]}\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z}/\widetilde{N}\mathbb{Z})}.
Remark.

This is known to be well-defined and independent of N~\widetilde{N}. Furthermore it is indeed a norm if s≥2s\geq 2; see [13, Lemma B.5].

We additionally recall the Gowers–Peluse norms which will be used when handling integer polynomial progressions.

Definition 2.4.

Given a function f:ℤ→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} with finite support and h,h′∈ℤh,h^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}, we define

(2.4) Δ(h,h′)​f​(x)=f⁡(x+h)​f⁡(x+h′)¯.\Delta_{(h,h^{\prime})}f(x)=f(x+h)\overline{f(x+h^{\prime})}.

Given a multiset Ω={μ1,…,μk}\Omega=\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{k}\} of probability measures on ℤ\mathbb{Z} and a positive integer scale N≥1N\geq 1, we define the Gowers–Peluse norms as

(2.5) ∥f∥UGP​[N;Ω]2k=∥f∥UGP​[N;μ1,…,μk]2k:=1N∑x∈ℤ𝔼hi,hi′∼μiΔ(h1,h1′)⋯Δ(hk,hk′)f(x).\lVert f\rVert_{U_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\Omega]}^{2^{k}}=\lVert f\rVert_{U_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{k}]}^{2^{k}}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{h_{i},h_{i}^{\prime}\sim\mu_{i}}\Delta_{(h_{1},h_{1}^{\prime})}\cdots\Delta_{(h_{k},h_{k}^{\prime})}f(x).

If Ω={μ,…,μ}\Omega=\{\mu,\ldots,\mu\} where the measure μ\mu is repeated kk times, we write that

∥f∥UGPk​[N;μ]=∥f∥UGP​[N;Ω].\lVert f\rVert_{U^{k}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\mu]}=\lVert f\rVert_{U_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\Omega]}.

When using the above definition, we will let μE\mu_{E} denote the uniform measure on a multiset EE for the sake of simplicity.

We now define the crucial counting operators which we will ultimately be used in our transference strategy. Recall that

P⁡(y)=∑j=d′dbj​yjP(y)=\sum_{j=d^{\prime}}^{d}b_{j}y^{j}

with bd′=1b_{d^{\prime}}=1, and recall the definitions of WW and PW​(y)P_{W}(y) from (2.1) and (2.2) respectively.

We will consider the following pair of operators. Given that these operators are rather more technical than the corresponding choices in (say) [39] we will provide motivation for the definitions after introducing them.

Definition 2.5.

Given functions fi:ℤ→ℂf_{i}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, i=1,…,ti=1,\ldots,t, we define the operator ΛW\Lambda_{W} as follows. Let

ΛW​(f1,…,ft)=𝔼z∼[1/2,1]​𝔼x∈[N]y∈[(z​N/(|bd|​Wd−d′))1/d]​∏i=1tfi​(x+ai​PW​(y)).\Lambda_{W}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim[1/2,1]}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N]\\ y\in[(zN/(|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}))^{1/d}]\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+a_{i}P_{W}(y)).

Let ε=bd/|bd|∈{±1}\varepsilon=b_{d}/|b_{d}|\in\{\pm 1\} and let

ν(y)=(d′d⋅(NW2)(d−d′)/(2​d​d′))⋅y−(d−d′)/d.\nu(y)=\Big(\frac{d^{\prime}}{d}\cdot\Big(\frac{N}{W^{2}}\Big)^{(d-d^{\prime})/(2dd^{\prime})}\Big)\cdot y^{-(d-d^{\prime})/d}.

We define the operator ΛModel\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}} by

ΛModel​(f1,…,ft)=𝔼x∈[N]y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]z∈[N1/2/2,N1/2]​ν​(y)⋅∏i=1tfi​(x+ai​(ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′).\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N]\\ y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\\ z\in[N^{1/2}/2,N^{1/2}]\end{subarray}}\nu(y)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+a_{i}(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}}).

To motivate these definitions, suppose for the sake of simplicity that we are attempting to transfer 33-term arithmetic progressions with common difference y2−y4y^{2}-y^{4}, that is, a→=(0,1,2)\vec{a}=(0,1,2) and P⁡(y)=y2−y4P(y)=y^{2}-y^{4}. A naive WW-trick compares counts of the pattern x,x+y2−W2​y4,x+2​(y2−W2​y4)x,x+y^{2}-W^{2}y^{4},x+2(y^{2}-W^{2}y^{4}) with that of x,x+y2,x+2​y2x,x+y^{2},x+2y^{2}. As yy grows, the sequence y2−W2​y4y^{2}-W^{2}y^{4} is far sparser than y2y^{2}; the weight ν⁡(y)\nu(y) is the corresponding archimedean correction factor (a nearly identical device is used in [39]). Observe however that when yy is large, y2−W2​y4y^{2}-W^{2}y^{4} is negative whereas y2y^{2} is positive. We correct this (without disturbing the WW-trick) by comparing with 33-APs with difference (−z​W+1)​y2(-zW+1)y^{2}. This however reintroduces an archimedian bias, which we then correct with the parameter zz in ΛW\Lambda_{W}.

Our next task will be to prove that ΛW\Lambda_{W} and ΛModel\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}} exhibit the appropriate Gowers norm control. We first obtain control on ΛW\Lambda_{W}; this is immediate given the results of Peluse [36, Theorem 6.1].

Lemma 2.6.

There exist integers s=s⁡(d,t)≥1s=s(d,t)\geq 1 and C=C⁡(d,t)≥1C=C(d,t)\geq 1 such that the following holds. Let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), fi:ℤ→ℂf_{i}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be 11-bounded functions supported on [±N][\pm N], N≥(δ−1​Wd)CN\geq(\delta^{-1}W^{d})^{C} and suppose that

|ΛW​(f1,…,ft)|≥δ.|\Lambda_{W}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})|\geq\delta.

Then

min1≤j≤t∥fj∥UGPs​[N;μWd−d′⋅[N/W(d−d′)]]≫P,a→δOd,t​(1).\min_{1\leq j\leq t}\lVert f_{j}\rVert_{U_{\operatorname{GP}}^{s}[N;\mu_{W^{d-d^{\prime}}\cdot[N/W^{(d-d^{\prime})}]}]}\gg_{P,\vec{a}}\delta^{O_{d,t}(1)}.

Note that the implicit constant here only depends on the coefficients of P⁡(y)P(y) and not on the coefficients of PW​(y)P_{W}(y).

Proof.

Let Mz=(z​N/(|bd|​Wd−d′))1/dM_{z}=(zN/(|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}))^{1/d}. Applying the triangle inequality we have that

𝔼z∈[1/2,1]​|𝔼x∈[N]y∈[Mz]​∏i=1tfi​(x+ai​PW​(y))|≥δ.\mathbb{E}_{z\in[1/2,1]}\Big|\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N]\\ y\in[M_{z}]\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+a_{i}P_{W}(y))\Big|\geq\delta.

Taking the supremum in zz, there exist z0z_{0} such that

|𝔼x∈[N]y∈[Mz0]​∏i=1tfi​(x+ai​PW​(y))|≥δ.\Big|\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N]\\ y\in[M_{z_{0}}]\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(x+a_{i}P_{W}(y))\Big|\geq\delta.

The desired result then follows from Theorem B.3 which is essentially an immediate consequence of [36, Theorem 6.1]. ∎

2.3. Nilsequence comparison result

The main algebraic computation in this section is proving that one may compare the orbit of a nilsequence on PW​(y)P_{W}(y) and (ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}}, and that the underlying averages will be close. This will be proven by iterative step–reduction, using the following equidistribution result of Leng [24, Theorem 4]. We refer the reader to Appendix A for relevant definitions.

Theorem 2.8.

Fix an integer ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, and let δ∈(0,1/10)\delta\in(0,1/10), M,D≥1M,D\geq 1. Suppose that GG is a dimension DD, at most ss-step connected, simply connected, nilpotent Lie group with a given degree kk filtration, and the nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma is complexity at most MM with respect to this filtration. Let F:G/Γ→ℂF\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C} and let gg be an ℓ\ell-variable polynomial sequence on GG with respect to this filtration.

Furthermore suppose that ∥F∥Lip≤1\lVert F\rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}}\leq 1 and FF has G(s)G_{(s)}-vertical frequency ξ\xi such that the height of ξ\xi is bounded by M/δM/\delta. Suppose that min1≤i≤ℓ⁡Ni≥(M/δ)Ok,ℓ​(DOk,ℓ​(1))\min_{1\leq i\leq\ell}N_{i}\geq(M/\delta)^{O_{k,\ell}(D^{O_{k,\ell}(1)})} and

|𝔼n→∈[N→]​F​(g⁡(n→)​Γ)|≥δ.\big|\mathbb{E}_{\vec{n}\in[\vec{N}]}F(g(\vec{n})\Gamma)\big|\geq\delta.

There exists an integer 0≤r≤dim(G/[G,G])0\leq r\leq\dim(G/[G,G]) such that:

  • •

    We have horizontal characters η1,…,ηr:G→ℝ\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{r}\colon G\to\mathbb{R} with heights bounded above by (M/δ)Ok,ℓ​(DOk,ℓ​(1))(M/\delta)^{O_{k,\ell}(D^{O_{k,\ell}(1)})},

  • •

    For all 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r, we have ∥ηi∘g∥C∞​[N→]≤(M/δ)Ok,ℓ​(DOk,ℓ​(1))\lVert\eta_{i}\circ g\rVert_{C^{\infty}[\vec{N}]}\leq(M/\delta)^{O_{k,\ell}(D^{O_{k,\ell}(1)})},

  • •

    For any w1,…,ws∈G/[G,G]w_{1},\ldots,w_{s}\in G/[G,G] such that wiw_{i} lie in the joint kernel of η1,…,ηr\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{r}, we have

    ξ⁡([[[w1,w2],w3],…,ws])=0.\xi([[[w_{1},w_{2}],w_{3}],\ldots,w_{s}])=0.

Our main result in this subsection is a uniform bound on pairs of nilsequence averages. Handling this problem via an iterative reduction to the case of abelian nilsequences is a key trick in this work, whereas previous approaches have worked directly at the level of fixed step nilsequences. In what follows we will call a congruence class ℓ\ell admissible if there exists yy such that PW​(y)≡ℓ​mod​Wd−d′P_{W}(y)\equiv\ell~\mathrm{mod}~W^{d-d^{\prime}}. We may also use this terminology for moduli other than Wd−d′W^{d-d^{\prime}}. Recall that PW​(y)P_{W}(y) has degree dd and leading coefficient |bd|​Wd−d′|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}. In the statement and throughout its proof below we treat dd as fixed (that is, we allow all constants to depend on dd).

Lemma 2.9.

Let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and F⁡(g⁡(n)​Γ)F(g(n)\Gamma) be a univariate nilsequence of degree kk, dimension DD and complexity MM. Furthermore suppose that maxi⁡|bi|≤M\max_{i}|b_{i}|\leq M, N≥WOk​(1)⋅(M/δ)Ok​(DOk​(1))N\geq W^{O_{k}(1)}\cdot(M/\delta)^{O_{k}(D^{O_{k}(1)})} and w≥(M/δ)Ok​(DOk​(1))w\geq(M/\delta)^{O_{k}(D^{O_{k}(1)})}.

Then for all ℓ∈[Wd−d′]\ell\in[W^{d-d^{\prime}}] which are admissible, we have that

|𝔼z∼[1/2,1]y∈[(z​N/(|bd|​Wd−d′))1/d]PW​(y)≡ℓ​mod​Wd−d′​F​(g⁡(PW​(y))​Γ)−𝔼y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]z∈[N1/2/2,N1/2](ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′≡ℓ​mod​Wd−d′​ν​(y)​F​(g⁡((ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′)​Γ)|≤δ.\displaystyle\bigg|\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\sim[1/2,1]\\ y\in[(zN/(|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}))^{1/d}]\\ P_{W}(y)\equiv\ell~\mathrm{mod}~W^{d-d^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}F(g(P_{W}(y))\Gamma)-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\\ z\in[N^{1/2}/2,N^{1/2}]\\ (\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}}\equiv\ell~\mathrm{mod}~W^{d-d^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}\nu(y)F(g((\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}})\Gamma)\bigg|\leq\delta.
Remark 2.10.

A slightly subtle point (which initially caused the authors substantial confusion) is that such a comparison is best handled by considering residue conditions for the polynomials PW​(y)P_{W}(y) and (ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}}, rather than for yy and zz separately. We note that this phenomenon does not arise when P⁡(y)P(y) has a simple root, in which case the the WW-trick is rather simpler (cf. the difference between Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 2.2).

Proof.

For the sake of simplicity, we will write Q⁡(z,y)=(ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′Q(z,y)=(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}} throughout. It will also be convenient to introduce the notation V:=|bd|​Wd−d′V:=|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}. Note that V|Wd−d′+1V|W^{d-d^{\prime}+1} since |bd|≤w|b_{d}|\leq w.

Step 1: Reducing to the case of linear exponential phases. We will proceed in an inductive manner by first iteratively reducing the step of the underlying nilmanifold to where the nilmanifold is abelian. At each stage of the iteration WiW_{i} will be a power of WW. We will have that ℓi\ell_{i} is an admissible residue class modulo WiW_{i}.

At each stage, we insist that gig_{i} is a polynomial sequence on GiG_{i}, that Gi/ΓiG_{i}/\Gamma_{i} has complexity MiM_{i}, and FiF_{i} has Lipschitz norm at most MiM_{i} and a vertical frequency ξi\xi_{i} of height at most MiM_{i}. Furthermore we assume that GiG_{i} has step sis_{i}, and that sis_{i} will decrease by 11 at each stage. We may assume ξi\xi_{i} is nonzero or else FiF_{i} descends to a function on the quotient Gi/(Gi)(si)G_{i}/(G_{i})_{(s_{i})} and we may immediately induct downward. Furthermore, we maintain that the underlying group GiG_{i} has dimension at most D+iD+i. Finally, note that at each iteration we may replace Fi​(gi​(n)​Γi)F_{i}(g_{i}(n)\Gamma_{i}) by updating the function to Fi​({gi​(0)}⋅Γ)F_{i}(\{g_{i}(0)\}\cdot\Gamma) and replacing the polynomial sequence by {gi​(0)}−1​g​(0)​[g⁡(0)]−1\{g_{i}(0)\}^{-1}g(0)[g(0)]^{-1} in order to guarantee that gi​(0)=idGig_{i}(0)=\operatorname{id}_{G_{i}} (one sees easily that doing so does not violate the shape of the complexity bounds). We will therefore assume that gi​(0)=idGig_{i}(0)=\operatorname{id}_{G_{i}} without loss of generality. We will inductively maintain the condition that ℓi\ell_{i} is a residue class modulo WiW_{i} such that

(2.7) |𝔼z∼[1/2,1]y∈[(z​N/V)1/d]PW​(y)≡ℓi​mod​Wi​Fi​(gi​(PW​(y))​Γi)−𝔼y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]z∈[N1/2/2,N1/2]Q⁡(z,y)≡ℓi​mod​Wi​ν​(y)​Fi​(gi​(Q⁡(z,y))​Γi)|≥τi.\displaystyle\bigg|\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\sim[1/2,1]\\ y\in[(zN/V)^{1/d}]\\ P_{W}(y)\equiv\ell_{i}~\mathrm{mod}~W_{i}\end{subarray}}F_{i}(g_{i}(P_{W}(y))\Gamma_{i})-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\\ z\in[N^{1/2}/2,N^{1/2}]\\ Q(z,y)\equiv\ell_{i}~\mathrm{mod}~W_{i}\end{subarray}}\nu(y)F_{i}(g_{i}(Q(z,y))\Gamma_{i})\bigg|\geq\tau_{i}.

Our induction will evolve the parameters via:

Mi+1\displaystyle M_{i+1} ≤(Mi/τi)Ok​(DOk​(1))\displaystyle\leq(M_{i}/\tau_{i})^{O_{k}(D^{O_{k}(1)})}
τi+1\displaystyle\tau_{i+1} ≥(Mi/τi)−Ok​(DOk​(1)).\displaystyle\geq(M_{i}/\tau_{i})^{-O_{k}(D^{O_{k}(1)})}.

We now proceed with the induction, beginning with (2.7). This implies that either

supz∈[1/2,1]|𝔼y∈[(z​N/V)1/d]PW​(y)≡ℓi​mod​Wi​Fi​(gi​(PW​(y))​Γi)|≥τi/2\displaystyle\sup_{z\in[1/2,1]}\bigg|\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in[(zN/V)^{1/d}]\\ P_{W}(y)\equiv\ell_{i}~\mathrm{mod}~W_{i}\end{subarray}}F_{i}(g_{i}(P_{W}(y))\Gamma_{i})\bigg|\geq\tau_{i}/2

2.4. Stashing and completing the proof

We now establish the crucial positivity property of ΛModel​(f,…,f)\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f,\ldots,f). In the following statement, implicit constants depend on d,a→d,\vec{a}.

Lemma 2.11.

Consider a function f:[N]→[0,1]f:[N]\to[0,1] with 𝔼⁡[f]≥δ\mathbb{E}[f]\geq\delta. We have the following bounds:

  • •

    Suppose that d′=1d^{\prime}=1 and t=3t=3. If N≥exp⁡(log⁡(1/δ)O⁡(1))N\geq\exp(\log(1/\delta)^{O(1)}), then

    ΛModel​(f,⋯,f)≥exp⁡(−(log⁡(1/δ))O⁡(1)).\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f,\cdots,f)\geq\exp(-(\log(1/\delta))^{O(1)}).
  • •

    Suppose that d′=1d^{\prime}=1 and t≥4t\geq 4. If N≥exp⁡(exp⁡(log⁡(1/δ)O⁡(1)))N\geq\exp(\exp(\log(1/\delta)^{O(1)})), then

    ΛModel​(f,⋯,f)≥exp⁡(−exp⁡(log⁡(1/δ)O⁡(1))).\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f,\cdots,f)\geq\exp(-\exp(\log(1/\delta)^{O(1)})).
  • •

    Suppose that d′>1d^{\prime}>1. If N≥exp⁡(exp⁡(1/δO⁡(1)))N\geq\exp(\exp(1/\delta^{O(1)})), then

    ΛModel​(f,⋯,f)≥exp⁡(−exp⁡(δ−O⁡(1))).\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f,\cdots,f)\geq\exp(-\exp(\delta^{-O(1)})).
Proof.

In each case it suffices to prove for all z∈[N1/2/2,N1/2]z\in[N^{1/2}/2,N^{1/2}] that

𝔼x∈[N]y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]​∏i=1tf⁡(x+ai​(ε⋅z​W+1)​yd′)\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N]\\ y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f(x+a_{i}(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}})

is suitably large. We have used here that ν(y)≫d1\nu(y)\gg_{d}1. Observe that we may break ff into progressions modulo |ε⋅z​W+1||\varepsilon\cdot zW+1| and be left with arithmetic progressions of length N1/2/WN^{1/2}/W. At least a δ/3\delta/3-fraction of these have average at least δ/3\delta/3 and hence breaking into these progressions, shifting and rescaling, it suffices to establish a lower bound for the operator

𝔼x∈[N1/2/W]y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]​∏i=1tf~​(x+ε⋅ai​yd′)\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[N^{1/2}/W]\\ y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\widetilde{f}(x+\varepsilon\cdot a_{i}y^{d^{\prime}})

where 𝔼x∈[N1/2/W]​f~​(x)≥δ/3\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N^{1/2}/W]}\widetilde{f}(x)\geq\delta/3. When d′=1d^{\prime}=1, this is a standard supersaturation argument for (essentially) arithmetic progressions. The first bound follows from (an essentially trivial) modification of the results of Kelley–Meka [16]. The second bound for t=4t=4 follows from (trivial adaptions to) work of Green–Tao [12] while the case of t≥5t\geq 5 follows from (trivial adaptions to) work of Leng, Sah and the second author [27]. The case d′>1d^{\prime}>1 follows from noting that supersaturation applies to the work of Prendiville [40]. Let τ=exp⁡(−exp⁡(δ−O⁡(1)))\tau=\exp(-\exp(\delta^{-O(1)})). In particular, choosing any m∈[τ⋅(N/W2)1/(2​d′)/2,τ⋅(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]m\in[\tau\cdot(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}/2,\tau\cdot(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}] we may break xx into progressions modulo md′m^{d^{\prime}} and consider yy which are multiples of mm. Observe that this gives a change of variable which preserves the pattern (precisely as we are in the homogeneous case). An Ω⁡(δ)\Omega(\delta)-fraction of these have average at least Ω⁡(δ)\Omega(\delta). Observe that these progressions have length τ−1\tau^{-1} and hence any progression with density Ω⁡(δ)\Omega(\delta) contains the desired pattern by [40, Theorem 1.1]. ∎

Remark 2.12.

It appears likely using that the configurations considered by Prendiville [40] are controlled by global Gowers norms via the results of Peluse [36], and thus that the results of [28] may be used to improve the obtained bounds. In particular, likely one may adopt the strategy in [27] by at each stage passing to progressions where one guarantees that the common difference is an appropriate perfect power. We leave the details to the interested reader.

We now state the quasipolynomial inverse theorem of Leng, Sah and the second author [28, Theorem 1.2]. Various conventions regarding nilsequences are discussed carefully in Appendix A; our conventions are completely standard.

Theorem 2.13.

Fix δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). Suppose that f:[N]→ℂf\colon[N]\to\mathbb{C} is 11-bounded and

∥f∥Us+1​[N]≥δ.\lVert f\rVert_{U^{s+1}[N]}\geq\delta.

Then there exists a nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma of degree ss, complexity at most MM, and dimension at most dd, a polynomial sequence g⁡(n)g(n) on GG, as well as a function FF on G/ΓG/\Gamma which is at most KK-Lipschitz such that

|𝔼n∈[N]​[f⁡(n)​F⁡(g⁡(n)​Γ)¯]|≥ε,|\mathbb{E}_{n\in[N]}[f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}]|\geq\varepsilon,

where we may take

d≤log⁡(1/δ)Os​(1)​​a​n​d​ε−1,K,M≤exp⁡(log⁡(1/δ)Os​(1)).d\leq\log(1/\delta)^{O_{s}(1)}\emph{and}\varepsilon^{-1},K,M\leq\exp(\log(1/\delta)^{O_{s}(1)}).

We now proceed to the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Proof.

Let w=(log⁡N)1/2w=(\log N)^{1/2} and recall that

W=∏p≤w(p,d)=1p⋅∏p≤w(p,d!)≠1p2​d⋅∏p≤w1/2pw1/3.W=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq w\\ (p,d)=1\end{subarray}}p\cdot\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq w\\ (p,d!)\neq 1\end{subarray}}p^{2d}\cdot\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq w^{1/2}\end{subarray}}p^{w^{1/3}}.

Standard elementary estimates yield that W≪d4wW\ll_{d}4^{w}, which is subpolynomial in NN.

We begin by supposing that fi:[N]→ℂf_{i}:[N]\to\mathbb{C} are 11-bounded and

|ΛW​(f1,…,ft)−ΛModel​(f1,…,ft)|≥δ.\Big|\Lambda_{W}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})-\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})\Big|\geq\delta.

Define

ΛDiff​(f1,…,ft):=ΛW​(f1,…,ft)−ΛModel​(f1,…,ft),\Lambda_{\operatorname{Diff}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}):=\Lambda_{W}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})-\Lambda_{\operatorname{Model}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}),

and

𝒟j\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{j} (f1,…,fj−1,fj+1,…,ft)​(x)\displaystyle(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{t})(x)
:=𝟙x∈[N]⋅(𝔼z∼[1/2,1]​𝔼y∈[(z​N/(|bd|​Wd−d′))1/d]​∏i∈[t]∖{j}fi​(x+(ai−aj)​PW​(y))CLOSE\displaystyle:=\mathbbm{1}_{x\in[N]}\cdot\Big(\mathbb{E}_{z\sim[1/2,1]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[(zN/(|b_{d}|W^{d-d^{\prime}}))^{1/d}]}\prod_{i\in[t]\setminus\{j\}}f_{i}(x+(a_{i}-a_{j})P_{W}(y))
−𝔼y∈[(N/W2)1/(2​d′)]z∈[N1/2/2,N1/2]ν(y)⋅∏i∈[t]∖{j}fi(x+(ai−aj)(ε⋅zW+1)yd′)).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in[(N/W^{2})^{1/(2d^{\prime})}]\\ z\in[N^{1/2}/2,N^{1/2}]\end{subarray}}\nu(y)\cdot\prod_{i\in[t]\setminus\{j\}}f_{i}(x+(a_{i}-a_{j})(\varepsilon\cdot zW+1)y^{d^{\prime}})\Big).

Observe that if fif_{i} are all supported on [N][N] then

ΛDiff​(f1,…,ft)=𝔼x∈[N]​𝒟j​(f1,…,fj−1,fj+1,…,ft)​(x)⋅fj​(x).\Lambda_{\operatorname{Diff}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathcal{D}_{j}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{t})(x)\cdot f_{j}(x).

This implies via Cauchy–Schwarz that

𝔼x∈[N]​[|𝒟j​(f1,…,fj−1,fj+1,…,ft)​(x)|2]≥δ2.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}[|\mathcal{D}_{j}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{t})(x)|^{2}]\geq\delta^{2}.

However, observe that

=ΛDiff​(f1,…,fj−1,𝒟j​(f1,…,fj−1,fj+1,…,ft)¯,fj+1,…,ft).\displaystyle=\Lambda_{\operatorname{Diff}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},\overline{\mathcal{D}_{j}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{t})},f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{t}).

Observe that combining Lemma 2.6 and Lemma 2.7, we obtain that there exists s=s⁡(d,t)≥1s=s(d,t)\geq 1 such that

or

Therefore we may apply the quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the Gowers norm [28, Theorem 1.2] combined with Lemma B.1 to deduce that there exists FjF_{j} which is 11-bounded and is a nilsequence of complexity exp⁡((log⁡(1/δ)O⁡(1))CLOSE\exp((\log(1/\delta)^{O(1)}) along each progression of common difference Wd−d′W^{d-d^{\prime}} and that

This previous set of manipulations (in particular defining the associated dual function and then applying Cauchy–Schwarz in this way) has been termed stashing by Manners [33].

Iterating this procedure from j=1j=1 to j=tj=t, we may obtain

3. Transference in finite fields

The main theorem for this section is the following result. By combining Theorem 3.1 with standard supersaturation results we will immediately be able to deduce Theorem 1.6. We omit the details of this deduction because they are essentially the same as in the previous section.

Theorem 3.1.

Let 𝒫=(x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y))\mathcal{P}=(x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y)) be a transferable polynomial pattern with Pi​(0)=0P_{i}(0)=0 for all ii. Let 𝒫∗:=(x+P1∗​(𝐲),…,x+Pt∗​(𝐲))\mathcal{P}^{\ast}:=(x+P_{1}^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{y}),\ldots,x+P_{t}^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{y})) denote the associated transferred (linear) pattern. Let fi:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf_{i}:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded for i=1,…,ti=1,\ldots,t and NN be prime. Then

|Λ𝒫​(f1,…,ft)−Λ𝒫∗​(f1,…,ft)|≤exp⁡(−c𝒫​(log⁡log⁡N)c𝒫).\left|\Lambda_{\mathcal{P}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})-\Lambda_{\mathcal{P}^{\ast}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})\right|\leq\exp(-c_{\mathcal{P}}(\log\log N)^{c_{\mathcal{P}}}).

3.1. Distributional tools

We now develop the distributional tools on nilsequences which will play a crucial role in the proof of Theorem 3.1. In this section we will ultimately derive our results using totally equidistributed nilsequences. Therefore we essentially rely on the equidistribution results of Green and Tao [14] (as quantified in [45]); we first require a periodic variant.

Fix an integer ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, δ∈(0,1/10)\delta\in(0,1/10), M,D≥1M,D\geq 1, and F:G/Γ→ℂF\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}. where g′g^{\prime} takes values G′G^{\prime} with dim⁡(G′)≤dim⁡(G)−1\operatorname{dim}(G^{\prime})\leq\operatorname{dim}(G)-1, γ⁡(n→)∈Γ\gamma(\vec{n})\in\Gamma and ε∈G\varepsilon\in G such that dG​(ε,idG)≤(M/δ)exp⁡(DOk,ℓ​(1))d_{G}(\varepsilon,\operatorname{id}_{G})\leq(M/\delta)^{\exp(D^{O_{k,\ell}(1)})}. Note that one may write g⁡(0→)={g⁡(0→)}​[g⁡(0→)]g(\vec{0})=\{g(\vec{0})\}[g(\vec{0})] with [g⁡(0→)]∈Γ[g(\vec{0})]\in\Gamma and ψG({g(0→)})∈[−1/2,1/2)D\psi_{G}(\{g(\vec{0})\})\in[-1/2,1/2)^{D} (the Mal’cev coordinates of the second kind). Observe that

Then the proof of [24, Lemma A.1] yields

where γ\gamma is QQ-periodic with Q≤(M/δ)exp⁡(DOk,ℓ​(1))Q\leq(M/\delta)^{\exp(D^{O_{k,\ell}(1)})}, g′​(0→)=γ⁡(0→)=0g^{\prime}(\vec{0})=\gamma(\vec{0})=0 and g′∈ker⁡(η)g^{\prime}\in\operatorname{ker}(\eta). We additionally require the following periodic factorization theorem.

Theorem 3.3.

Fix A≥2A\geq 2. Suppose that GG is a dimension DD simply connected nilpotent Lie group with a given degree kk filtration, and the nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma is complexity at most M′M^{\prime} with respect to this filtration.     g=g′​γg=g^{\prime}\gamma with g′​(0)=γ⁡(0)=idGg^{\prime}(0)=\gamma(0)=\operatorname{id}_{G}, and g′g^{\prime} is NN-periodic on G′/(G′∩Γ)G^{\prime}/(G^{\prime}\cap\Gamma),

    G′G^{\prime} is an MM-rational subgroup of GG and G′/Γ′G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime} has a Mal’cev basis 𝒳′\mathcal{X}^{\prime} which comprises MM-rational combinations of the Mal’cev basis 𝒳\mathcal{X} of G/ΓG/\Gamma,

    Let g′=g1n⋯gknkg^{\prime}=g_{1}^{n}\cdots g_{k}^{n^{k}}. For each nonzero ii-th horizontal character η\eta of height at most MAM^{A} on G′G^{\prime} (given filtration Gi′=G′∩GiG_{i}^{\prime}=G^{\prime}\cap G_{i}) we have that

    ∥η⁡(gi)∥ℝ/ℤ≥MA⋅N−i,\lVert\eta(g_{i})\rVert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\geq M^{A}\cdot N^{-i},

    γ\gamma takes values only in Γ\Gamma.

Proof.

A qualitative version of this proposition appears as [4, Proposition 5.2]. For the quantitative bound, [45, Theorem A.6] tracks the quantitative details of the nonperiodic analogous factorization algorithm from [14] and inputting Theorem 3.2, we get the stated quantitative bounds. ∎

We now come to the crux of this section regarding the equidistribution of transferable polynomial patterns. We remark that we operate essentially throughout with the Lie algebra as in [1].

Theorem 3.4.

Let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), suppose that GG is a dimension DD simply connected nilpotent Lie group with a given degree kk filtration and the nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma is complexity at most MM with respect to this filtration. Let gg be an NN-periodic polynomial sequence with respect to this filtration with g⁡(0)=idGg(0)=\operatorname{id}_{G} and N≥(M/δ)exp⁡(O𝒫​(DOk​(1)))N\geq(M/\delta)^{\exp(O_{\mathcal{P}}(D^{O_{k}(1)}))}.

Let 𝒫=(x+P1​(y),…,x+Pt​(y))\mathcal{P}=(x+P_{1}(y),\ldots,x+P_{t}(y)) be a transferable polynomial pattern with Pi​(0)=0P_{i}(0)=0. Let Ψ:=𝒫∗\Psi:=\mathcal{P}^{\ast} denote the transferred pattern. Let GΨ/ΓΨG^{\Psi}/\Gamma^{\Psi} denote the corresponding Leibman nilmanifold.

Consider an MM-Lipschitz function F:GΨ/ΓΨ→ℂF:G^{\Psi}/\Gamma^{\Psi}\to\mathbb{C} such that

(3.1) |𝔼x,y∈ℤ/N​ℤ​F​((,,,,,))−∫GΨ/ΓΨF|≥δ.\bigg|\mathbb{E}_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}F((g(x+P_{1}(y)),\ldots,g(x+P_{t}(y))))-\int_{G^{\Psi}/\Gamma^{\Psi}}F\bigg|\geq\delta.

Let the Taylor expansion of g⁡(n)g(n) be

g⁡(n)=∏j=1kgjnj.g(n)=\prod_{j=1}^{k}g_{j}^{n^{j}}.

Then there exists a nontrivial ℓ\ell-th horizontal character ηℓ\eta_{\ell} of height at most ≤(M/δ)exp⁡(O𝒫​(DOk​(1)))\leq(M/\delta)^{\exp(O_{\mathcal{P}}(D^{O_{k}(1)}))} such that

∥ηℓ​(gℓ)∥ℝ/ℤ=0.\lVert\eta_{\ell}(g_{\ell})\rVert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}=0.
Proof.

Let

g⁡(n)=exp⁡(∑ℓ=1kg~i​ni),g(n)=\exp\bigg(\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\widetilde{g}_{i}n^{i}\bigg),

with g~i∈𝔤ℓ:=log⁡(Gℓ)\widetilde{g}_{i}\in\mathfrak{g}_{\ell}:=\log(G_{\ell}); that is, 𝔤ℓ\mathfrak{g}_{\ell} is the Lie algebra associated with GℓG_{\ell}.

We will frequently need to operate within the Lie algebra 𝔤t:=log⁡(G)t\mathfrak{g}^{t}:=\log(G)^{t}. We identify this vector space with 𝔤⊗ℝt\mathfrak{g}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{t} via the following map on elementary tensors (in the backwards direction)

a⊗v↦(v1​a,…,vt​a).a\otimes v\mapsto(v_{1}a,\ldots,v_{t}a).

Note that under this identification we inherit the Lie bracket operation

[a⊗v1,b⊗v2]=[a,b]⊗v1​v2,[a\otimes v_{1},b\otimes v_{2}]=[a,b]\otimes v_{1}v_{2},

where the final product is entrywise.

Recall that

GΨ=⟨gℓvℓ:gℓ∈Gℓ,vℓ∈Ψ[ℓ]⟩.G^{\Psi}=\langle g_{\ell}^{v_{\ell}}:g_{\ell}\in G_{\ell},v_{\ell}\in\Psi^{[\ell]}\rangle.

To see that (g⁡(x+P1​(y)),…,g⁡(x+Pt​(y)))(g(x+P_{1}(y)),\ldots,g(x+P_{t}(y))) takes values in GΨG^{\Psi}, we just need to observe that ((x+P1​(y))ℓ,…,(x+Pt​(y))ℓ)((x+P_{1}(y))^{\ell},\ldots,(x+P_{t}(y))^{\ell}) lies in Ψ[ℓ]\Psi^{[\ell]} for each ℓ\ell. But this is clear since

{((x+P1​(y))ℓ,…,(x+Pt​(y))ℓ)}x,y∈ℤ⊂{((x+P1∗​(𝒚))ℓ,…,(x+Pt∗​(𝒚))ℓ)}x∈ℤ,𝒚∈ℤD.\{((x+P_{1}(y))^{\ell},\ldots,(x+P_{t}(y))^{\ell})\}_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}}\subset\{((x+P_{1}^{*}(\boldsymbol{y}))^{\ell},\ldots,(x+P_{t}^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{y}))^{\ell})\}_{x\in\mathbb{Z},\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^{D}}.

We now note that the complexity of GΨ/ΓΨG^{\Psi}/\Gamma^{\Psi} can easily be bounded by MO𝒫​(DOk​(1))M^{O_{\mathcal{P}}(D^{O_{k}(1)})}. 3.2. Proof of Theorem 3.1

We first recall the statement of the inverse theorem over ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}.

Theorem 3.5.

Fix δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). Suppose that f:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} is 11-bounded and

∥f∥Us+1​[N]≥δ.\lVert f\rVert_{U^{s+1}[N]}\geq\delta.

Then there exists a nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma of degree ss, complexity at most MM, and dimension at most DD, an NN-periodic polynomial sequence g⁡(n)g(n) on GG, as well as a function FF on G/ΓG/\Gamma which is at most KK-Lipschitz such that

|𝔼n∈ℤ/N​ℤ​[f⁡(n)​F⁡(g⁡(n)​Γ)¯]|≥ε,|\mathbb{E}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}[f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}]|\geq\varepsilon,

where we may take

D≤log⁡(1/δ)Os​(1)​​a​n​d​ε−1,K,M≤exp⁡(log⁡(1/δ)Os​(1)).D\leq\log(1/\delta)^{O_{s}(1)}\emph{and}\varepsilon^{-1},K,M\leq\exp(\log(1/\delta)^{O_{s}(1)}).
Proof.

The only difference in this statement versus that of Theorem 2.13 is that we insist that the underlying polynomial sequence is NN-periodic. This is accomplished via an argument of Manners [31]. The precise quantitative details are exactly as in [29, Theorem C.3] modulo changing the subscripts U4U^{4} to Us+1U^{s+1} (the primary technical work of quantifying the construction of Manners is carried out in the appropriately generality in [29, Proposition C.2]). ∎

We are ready to prove Theorem 3.1. Aspects of the strategy that are similar to what has been seen before are treated with some brevity.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

For i=1,…,ti=1,\ldots,t, define the dual functions

𝒟i​(x):=𝔼y,𝒚​∏j≠ifi​(x+Pj​(y)−Pi​(y))−∏j≠ifi​(x+Pj∗​(𝒚)−Pi∗​(𝒚)).\mathcal{D}_{i}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{y,\boldsymbol{y}}\prod_{j\neq i}f_{i}(x+P_{j}(y)-P_{i}(y))-\prod_{j\neq i}f_{i}(x+P^{\ast}_{j}(\boldsymbol{y})-P^{\ast}_{i}(\boldsymbol{y})).

δ:=|Λ𝒫​(f1,…,ft)−Λ𝒫∗​(f1,…,ft)|.\delta:=\left|\Lambda_{\mathcal{P}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})-\Lambda_{\mathcal{P}^{\ast}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})\right|.

Appendix A Conventions regarding nilsequences

We begin this appendix by giving the precise definition of the complexity of a nilmanifold; this definition is exactly as in [45, Definition 6.1].

Definition A.1.

Let s≥1s\geq 1 be an integer and let K>0K>0. A filtered nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma of degree ss and complexity at most KK consists of the following:

  • •

    a nilpotent, connected, and simply connected Lie group GG of dimension mm, which can be identified with its Lie algebra log⁡G\log G via the exponential map exp:log⁡G→G\exp\colon\log G\to G;

  • •

    a filtration G∙=(Gi)i≥0G_{\bullet}=(G_{i})_{i\geq 0} of closed connected subgroups GiG_{i} of GG with

    G=G0=G1⩾G1⩾⋯⩾Gs⩾Gs+1=IdGG=G_{0}=G_{1}\geqslant G_{1}\geqslant\cdots\geqslant G_{s}\geqslant G_{s+1}=\mathrm{Id}_{G}

    such that [Gi,Gj]⊆Gi+j[G_{i},G_{j}]\subseteq G_{i+j} for all i,j≥0i,j\geq 0 (equivalently [log⁡Gi,log⁡Gj]⊆log⁡Gi+j[\log G_{i},\log G_{j}]\subseteq\log G_{i+j});

  • •

    a discrete cocompact subgroup Γ\Gamma of GG; and

  • •

    a linear basis 𝒳={X1,…,Xm}\mathcal{X}=\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{m}\} of log⁡G\log G, known as a Mal’cev basis.

We, furthermore, require that this data obeys the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    for 1≤i,j≤m1\leq i,j\leq m, one has Lie algebra relations

    [Xi,Xj]=∑i,j<k≤mci​j​k​Xk[X_{i},X_{j}]=\sum_{i,j<k\leq m}c_{ijk}X_{k}

    for rational numbers ci​j​kc_{ijk} of height at most KK (we will often refer to these as the Lie bracket structure constants);

  2. (2)

    for each 1≤i≤s1\leq i\leq s, the Lie algebra log⁡Gi\log G_{i} is spanned by {Xj:m−dim(Gi)<j≤m}\{X_{j}\colon m-\dim(G_{i})<j\leq m\}; and

  3. (3)

    the subgroup Γ\Gamma consists of all elements of the form exp(t1X1)⋯exp(tmXm)\exp(t_{1}X_{1})\cdots\exp(t_{m}X_{m}) with ti∈ℤt_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}.

We note that the conditions imply [G,Gs]=IdG[G,G_{s}]=\mathrm{Id}_{G}, i.e., GsG_{s} is contained in the center of GG (commutes with every element).

Next, we will define polynomial sequences in filtered nilpotent groups. This concrete definition is equivalent (by [14, Lemma 6.7]) to the one given in [14].

Definition A.2.

We adopt the conventions of Definition A.1. Let GG be a filtered nilpotent group of degree ss. A function g:ℤ→Gg\colon\mathbb{Z}\to G is a polynomial sequence if there exist elements gi∈Gig_{i}\in G_{i} for i=0,…,si=0,\ldots,s such that

g(n)=g0g1(n1)⋯gs(ns),g(n)=g_{0}g_{1}^{\binom{n}{1}}\cdots g_{s}^{\binom{n}{s}},

where (ni)=1i!​∏j=0i−1(n−j)\binom{n}{i}=\frac{1}{i!}\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(n-j), for all n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. We say a polynomial sequence g⁡(n)g(n) is NN-periodic with respect to a lattice Γ\Gamma if

g⁡(n)​g​(n+N)−1∈Γg(n)g(n+N)^{-1}\in\Gamma

for all n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}.

We will denote the set of polynomial sequences g:ℤ→Gg\colon\mathbb{Z}\to G relative to the filtration G∙G_{\bullet} of GG by poly⁡(ℤ,G∙)\operatorname{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G_{\bullet}). It turns out that poly⁡(ℤ,G∙)\operatorname{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G_{\bullet}) is a group under the natural multiplication of sequences–this is due to Lazard [21] and Leibman [22, 23].

Now we can define Mal’cev coordinates, the explicit metrics on GG and G/ΓG/\Gamma used in our work, and the precise definition of the Lipschitz norm of functions on G/ΓG/\Gamma. These definitions are exactly as in [14, Appendix A].

Definition A.3.

We adopt the conventions of Definition A.1. Given a Mal’cev basis 𝒳\mathcal{X} and g∈Gg\in G, there exists (t1,…,tm)∈ℝm(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that

g=exp⁡(t1​X1+t2​X2+…​tm​Xm).g=\exp(t_{1}X_{1}+t_{2}X_{2}+\ldots t_{m}X_{m}).

We define Mal’cev coordinates of first kind ψexp=ψexp,𝒳:G→ℝm\psi_{\exp}=\psi_{\exp,\mathcal{X}}\colon G\to\mathbb{R}^{m} for gg relative to 𝒳\mathcal{X} by

ψexp​(g):=(t1,…,tm).\psi_{\exp}(g):=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}).

Given g∈Gg\in G there also exists (u1,…,um)∈ℝm(u_{1},\ldots,u_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that

g=exp(u1X1)⋯exp(umXm),g=\exp(u_{1}X_{1})\cdots\exp(u_{m}X_{m}),

and we define the Mal’cev coordinates of second kind ψ=ψ𝒳:G→ℝm\psi=\psi_{\mathcal{X}}\colon G\to\mathbb{R}^{m} for gg relative to 𝒳\mathcal{X} by

ψ⁡(g):=(u1,…,um).\psi(g):=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}).

We then define a metric d=d𝒳d=d_{\mathcal{X}} on GG by

d(x,y):=inf{∑i=1nmin(∥ψ(xixi+1−1)∥,∥ψ(xi+1xi−1)∥):n∈ℕ,x1,…,xn+1∈G,x1=x,xn+1=y},d(x,y):=\inf\bigg\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min(\lVert\psi(x_{i}x_{i+1}^{-1})\rVert,\lVert\psi(x_{i+1}x_{i}^{-1})\rVert)\colon n\in\mathbb{N},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n+1}\in G,x_{1}=x,x_{n+1}=y\bigg\},

where ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}-norm on ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, and define a metric on G/ΓG/\Gamma by

d⁡(x​Γ,y​Γ)=infγ,γ′∈Γd⁡(x​γ,y​γ′).d(x\Gamma,y\Gamma)=\inf_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma}d(x\gamma,y\gamma^{\prime}).

Furthermore, for any function F:G/Γ→ℂF\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}, we define

∥F∥Lip:=∥F∥∞+supx,y∈G/Γx≠y|F⁡(x)−F⁡(y)|d⁡(x,y).\lVert F\rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}}:=\lVert F\rVert_{\infty}+\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in G/\Gamma\\ x\neq y\end{subarray}}\frac{|F(x)-F(y)|}{d(x,y)}.

We recall the notion of a horizontal character and the notion of a function FF having a vertical frequency; our definitions are exactly as in [14, Definitions 1.5, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5].

Definition A.4.

Given a filtered nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma, the horizontal torus is defined to be

(G/Γ)ab:=G/[G,G]​Γ.(G/\Gamma)_{\mathrm{ab}}:=G/[G,G]\Gamma.

A horizontal character is a continuous homomorphism η:G→ℝ/ℤ\eta\colon G\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} that annihilates Γ\Gamma; such characters may be equivalently viewed as characters on the horizontal torus. A horizontal character is nontrivial if it is not identically zero.

Furthermore, if the nilmanifold G/ΓG/\Gamma has degree ss, the vertical torus is defined to be

Gs/(Gs∩Γ).G_{s}/(G_{s}\cap\Gamma).

A vertical character is a continuous homomorphism ξ:Gs→ℝ/ℤ\xi\colon G_{s}\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} that annihilates Γ∩Gs\Gamma\cap G_{s}. Setting ms=dimGsm_{s}=\dim G_{s}, one may use the last msm_{s} coordinates of the Mal’cev coordinate map to identify GsG_{s} and Gs/(Gs∩Γ)G_{s}/(G_{s}\cap\Gamma) with ℝms\mathbb{R}^{m_{s}} and ℝms/ℤms\mathbb{R}^{m_{s}}/\mathbb{Z}^{m_{s}}, respectively. Thus, we may identify any vertical character ξ\xi with a unique k∈ℤmsk\in\mathbb{Z}^{m_{s}} such that ξ⁡(x)=k⋅x\xi(x)=k\cdot x under this identification Gs/(Γ∩Gs)≅ℝms/ℤmsG_{s}/(\Gamma\cap G_{s})\cong\mathbb{R}^{m_{s}}/\mathbb{Z}^{m_{s}}. We refer to kk as the frequency of the character ξ\xi, we write |ξ|:=∥k∥∞|\xi|:=\lVert k\rVert_{\infty} to denote the magnitude of the frequency ξ\xi, and say that a function F:G/Γ→ℂF\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C} has a vertical frequency ξ\xi if

F⁡(gs⋅x)=e⁡(ξ⁡(gs))​F​(x)F(g_{s}\cdot x)=e(\xi(g_{s}))F(x)

for all gs∈Gsg_{s}\in G_{s} and x∈G/Γx\in G/\Gamma. We may also refer to |ξ||\xi| as the height of ξ\xi.

We will also need the following notion of smoothness of polynomials which take values in the torus.

Definition A.5.

Let p:ℤℓ→ℝ/ℤp:\mathbb{Z}^{\ell}\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} be a polynomial of the form

p⁡(n→)=∑j→αj→​(n→j→),p(\vec{n})=\sum_{\vec{j}}\alpha_{\vec{j}}\binom{\vec{n}}{\vec{j}},

where (n→j→)=∏i=1ℓ(niji)\binom{\vec{n}}{\vec{j}}=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n_{i}}{j_{i}}. Then, for N1,…,Nℓ∈ℕN_{1},\ldots,N_{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}, define:

∥p∥C∞​[N→]:=supj→≠0→∥αj→∥ℝ/ℤ​N→j→,\lVert p\rVert_{C^{\infty}[\vec{N}]}:=\sup_{\vec{j}\neq\vec{0}}\lVert\alpha_{\vec{j}}\rVert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\vec{N}^{\vec{j}},

where N→j→=∏i=1ℓNiji\vec{N}^{\vec{j}}=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}N_{i}^{j_{i}}.

We finally record the following technical lemma about coefficients of polynomial sequences when lifted to the Lie algebra.

Lemma A.6.

Let GG have a degree kk filtration G∙G_{\bullet} and g(n)=g1n⋯gknkg(n)=g_{1}^{n}\cdots g_{k}^{n^{k}} be a polynomial sequence adapted to G∙G_{\bullet}. Let 𝔤\mathfrak{g} be the Lie algebra of GG and 𝔤∙\mathfrak{g}_{\bullet} be the corresponding filtration. Then log⁡(g⁡(n)):=∑ℓ=1kg~ℓ​nℓ\log(g(n)):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\widetilde{g}_{\ell}n^{\ell} is a polynomial sequence adapted to 𝔤∙\mathfrak{g}_{\bullet} and

exp⁡(aℓ)=gℓmod⟨Gℓ+1,[Gj,Gℓ−j]⟩,\exp(a_{\ell})=g_{\ell}\mod\langle G_{\ell+1},[G_{j},G_{\ell-j}]\rangle,

for all ℓ\ell.

Proof.

That log⁡(g⁡(n))\log(g(n)) is adapted to 𝔤∙\mathfrak{g}_{\bullet} is an easy induction using the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula. For each ℓ\ell, let 𝔥ℓ\mathfrak{h}_{\ell} be the smallest Lie subalgebra of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} containing 𝔤ℓ+1\mathfrak{g}_{\ell+1} and [𝔤j,𝔤ℓ−j][\mathfrak{g}_{j},\mathfrak{g}_{\ell-j}]. The following consequence of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula was observed in [1, Lemma 5.8]: for univariate polynomial sequences q,q′q,q^{\prime} in 𝔤\mathfrak{g} adapted to 𝔤∙\mathfrak{g}_{\bullet}, we have

(log⁡(exp⁡(q)​exp⁡(q′)))ℓ=(q)ℓ+(q′)ℓmod𝔥ℓ,(\log(\exp(q)\exp(q^{\prime})))_{\ell}=(q)_{\ell}+(q^{\prime})_{\ell}\mod\mathfrak{h}_{\ell},

where (q)ℓ(q)_{\ell} denotes the coefficient of the degree ℓ\ell term of qq. Iterating this we see that see that for each ℓ\ell

g~ℓ=(log⁡(∏i=1kgini))ℓ=∑i=1k(log⁡(gini))ℓmod𝔥ℓ=log⁡(gℓ)mod𝔥ℓ.\widetilde{g}_{\ell}=(\log(\prod_{i=1}^{k}g_{i}^{n^{i}}))_{\ell}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\log(g_{i}^{n^{i}}))_{\ell}\mod\mathfrak{h}_{\ell}=\log(g_{\ell})\mod\mathfrak{h}_{\ell}.

Exponentiating yields the result. ∎

The sum on the left is over a subset of all pairs (hj,hj′)(h_{j},h^{\prime}_{j}) with hj,hj′∈[±3​N]h_{j},h^{\prime}_{j}\in[\pm 3N], with the weight attached to each pair being (2​N+1)−1​(4​N+1)−1≤5​(6​N+1)−2(2N+1)^{-1}(4N+1)^{-1}\leq 5(6N+1)^{-2}. It follows (using the nonnegativity of the inner sum over x,h1,…,hj−1x,h_{1},\dots,h_{j-1}) that

𝔼hj,hj′∼μ~\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{h_{j},h_{j}^{\prime}\sim\tilde{\mu}} ∑x,h1,…,hj−1∈ℤ𝔼hi,hi′∼μ~j+1≤i≤sΔh1⋯Δhj−1Δ(hj+1,hj+1′)⋯Δ(hs,hs′)(Δ(hj,hj′)f(x))≥5−1cj−sδ2sNj≥cj−s−1δ2sNj.\displaystyle\sum_{x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{j-1}\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}h_{i},h_{i}^{\prime}\sim\tilde{\mu}\\ j+1\leq i\leq s\end{subarray}}\Delta_{h_{1}}\cdots\Delta_{h_{j-1}}\Delta_{(h_{j+1},h_{j+1}^{\prime})}\cdots\Delta_{(h_{s},h_{s}^{\prime})}(\Delta_{(h_{j},h_{j}^{\prime})}f(x))\geq 5^{-1}c^{j-s}\delta^{2^{s}}N^{j}\geq c^{j-s-1}\delta^{2^{s}}N^{j}.

This is B.1 in the case j−1j-1 and thus completes the proof of the inductive step, and hence of item (i) in the lemma. ∎

We next require the following standard Fourier approximation lemma.

Lemma B.2.

Let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and N≥δ−1N\geq\delta^{-1}. There exists Gδ:ℤ→[0,1]G_{\delta}:\mathbb{Z}\to[0,1] such that

∫Θ|Gδ^​(Θ)|\displaystyle\int_{\Theta}|\widehat{G_{\delta}}(\Theta)| ≪δ​log⁡(1/δ)\displaystyle\ll\delta\log(1/\delta)
Gδ​(x)\displaystyle G_{\delta}(x) =1​ for ​x∈[δ​N,(1−δ)​N]\displaystyle=1\text{ for }x\in[\delta N,(1-\delta)N]
Gδ​(x)\displaystyle G_{\delta}(x) =0​ for ​x∉[−δ​N,(1+δ)​N].\displaystyle=0\text{ for }x\notin[-\delta N,(1+\delta)N].
Proof.

Let

Gδ​(x)=𝟙[⋅∈[N]]∗𝟙[⋅∈[δ⋅N]]2​⌊δ​N⌋+1.G_{\delta}(x)=\frac{\mathbbm{1}[\cdot\in[N]]\ast\mathbbm{1}[\cdot\in[\delta\cdot N]]}{2\lfloor\delta N\rfloor+1}.

As

𝟙[⋅∈[X]]^​(Θ)≪min⁡(X,∥Θ∥ℝ/ℤ−1)\widehat{\mathbbm{1}[\cdot\in[X]]}(\Theta)\ll\min(X,\lVert\Theta\rVert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^{-1})

the result follows via direct integration. ∎

We next recall a special case of [36, Theorem 6.1] which will serve as the primary PET control statement over the integers for our work.

Theorem B.3.

Let N≥1N\geq 1, C≥1C\geq 1, 1≤d′≤d1\leq d^{\prime}\leq d and a1,…,at∈ℤa_{1},\ldots,a_{t}\in\mathbb{Z} be distinct integers. Let ℓ\ell be a nonzero integer.

Let fi:[±N]→ℂf_{i}:[\pm N]\to\mathbb{C}, P⁡(y)=∑j=d′dbi​yj∈ℤ⁡[y]P(y)=\sum_{j=d^{\prime}}^{d}b_{i}y^{j}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] with bd′≠0b_{d^{\prime}}\neq 0 and define PW​(y)=W−d′​P​(W​y)P_{W}(y)=W^{-d^{\prime}}P(Wy). Suppose that maxi⁡|bi|≤C\max_{i}|b_{i}|\leq C, maxi⁡|ai|≤C\max_{i}|a_{i}|\leq C, that M​(|ℓ|⋅W−d+d′/N)1/d∈[1/C,C]M(|\ell|\cdot W^{-d+d^{\prime}}/N)^{1/d}\in[1/C,C] and that

∑x∈[N]∑y∈[M]f1(x+a1⋅ℓPW(y))⋯ft(x+at⋅ℓPW(y))≥δNM.\sum_{x\in[N]}\sum_{y\in[M]}f_{1}(x+a_{1}\cdot\ell P_{W}(y))\cdots f_{t}(x+a_{t}\cdot\ell P_{W}(y))\geq\delta NM.

Let μ~\widetilde{\mu} denote the uniform measure on ℓWd−d′⋅[±N/(ℓ⋅Wd−d′)]\ell W^{d-d^{\prime}}\cdot[\pm N/(\ell\cdot W^{d-d^{\prime}})]. Then there exists s=s⁡(d,t)≥2s=s(d,t)\geq 2 such that

mini∈[t]∥fi∥UGPs⁡[N;μ~]≫CδOd,t​(1).\min_{i\in[t]}\lVert f_{i}\rVert_{U_{\operatorname{GP}^{s}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}}\gg_{C}\delta^{O_{d,t}(1)}.
Proof.

There are several slight technical differences between Theorem B.3 and the statement appearing in [36, Theorem 6.1]; we perform the necessary maneuvers to reduce to the statement there.

If ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0 for all ii, we encode the x∈[N]x\in[N] via introducing a function ft+1(x)=𝟙[x∈[N]]f_{t+1}(x)=\mathbbm{1}[x\in[N]] and adding at+1=0a_{t+1}=0. If there exits ai=0a_{i}=0, we replace fif_{i} by fi~(x)=fi(x)⋅𝟙[x∈[N]]\widetilde{f_{i}}(x)=f_{i}(x)\cdot\mathbbm{1}[x\in[N]]. Observe that if ∥fi~∥UGPs​[N;μ~]≥δ′\lVert\widetilde{f_{i}}\rVert_{U^{s}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}\geq\delta^{\prime} then taking δ′′=δ′Os​(1)\delta^{\prime\prime}=\delta^{\prime O_{s}(1)} we have that ∥fi⋅Gδ′′∥UGPs​[N;μ~]≥δ′/2\lVert f_{i}\cdot G_{\delta^{\prime\prime}}\rVert_{U^{s}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}\geq\delta^{\prime}/2 using Lemma B.2. Via applying Fourier inversion Gδ​(x)=∫01Gδ^​(Θ)​e​(Θ​x)​𝑑ΘG_{\delta}(x)=\int_{0}^{1}\widehat{G_{\delta}}(\Theta)e(\Theta x)~d\Theta and using that the Gowers–Peluse norm satisfies triangle inequality, we have supΘ∥fi⋅e(Θ⋅)∥UGPs​[N;μ~]≥(δ′)Os​(1)\sup_{\Theta}\lVert f_{i}\cdot e(\Theta\cdot)\rVert_{U^{s}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}\geq(\delta^{\prime})^{O_{s}(1)}. As s≥2s\geq 2, a direct computation gives ∥fi⋅e(Θ⋅)∥UGPs​[N;μ~]=∥fi∥UGPs​[N;μ~]\lVert f_{i}\cdot e(\Theta\cdot)\rVert_{U^{s}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}=\lVert f_{i}\rVert_{U^{s}_{\operatorname{GP}}[N;\widetilde{\mu}]}. Therefore it suffices to operate under the alternate assumption that

∑x∈ℤ∑y∈[M]f1(x+a1⋅ℓPW(y))⋯ft(x+at⋅ℓPW(y))≥δNM.\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{y\in[M]}f_{1}(x+a_{1}\cdot\ell P_{W}(y))\cdots f_{t}(x+a_{t}\cdot\ell P_{W}(y))\geq\delta NM.

Observe that in this situation, by changing variables x→x+2​ℓ⋅maxi⁡|ai|​PW​(y)x\to x+2\ell\cdot\max_{i}|a_{i}|P_{W}(y) we may additionally assume that ai>0a_{i}>0. Given these shifted constraints, we may additionally add f0(x)=𝟙[x∈[4C2N]]f_{0}(x)=\mathbbm{1}[x\in[4C^{2}N]].

We then apply [36, Theorem 6.1] with N′=4​C2​NN^{\prime}=4C^{2}N and MM as defined and obtain that

We now state the version of PET control which is required for Section 3; the statement we require appears as [35, Proposition 2.2].

Theorem B.4.

Let P1​(y),…,Pm​(y)∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1}(y),\ldots,P_{m}(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be pairwise distinct polynomials and f1,…,fm:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be 11-bounded. Then there exists s=s⁡(P1,…,Pm)≥1s=s(P_{1},\ldots,P_{m})\geq 1, β=β⁡(P1,…,Pm)∈(0,1]\beta=\beta(P_{1},\ldots,P_{m})\in(0,1] such that

|𝔼⁡[∏i=1mfi​(x+Pi​(y))]|≤mini⁡∥fi∥Us​(ℤ/N​ℤ)β+O𝒫​(N−β).\Big|\mathbb{E}\Big[\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(x+P_{i}(y))\Big]\Big|\leq\min_{i}\lVert f_{i}\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})}^{\beta}+O_{\mathcal{P}}(N^{-\beta}).
